PUBLIC TRANSCRIPTION — NOT THE ORIGINAL SENT-ITEM FILE

PUBLIC TRANSCRIPTION FROM A LATER QUOTATION — NOT THE ORIGINAL SENT-ITEM FILE
Record: GHF-E170 / 21 September 2026 request
Date: 21 September 2026 (the page also records a reference in the text to a 20 September request date)
Sender: Sion Buckler
Timestamp: not independently verified from original headers

Dr Misra,

Thank you for replying, and for doing so promptly and at a weekend. Good
drills Sir. What an honour. I know you and the Council serve as volunteers,
and I am grateful for the time.

Let me set out plainly what I am asking of the Council, which is narrow.
If you'll allow me?

I am not asking your Council to revisit Mr Egan's answer of 14 June 2026.
He explained that the minute books from 1982 onwards were deposited with
Glamorgan Archives in 2002, and I am pursuing those there.

What I am asking about is what that answer did not cover. Llandough
Community Council is a public authority under Schedule 1, Part II,
paragraph 7(b) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000. The Act applies to
the recorded information set out below generally; the Environmental
Information Regulations 2004 apply in addition to any part of it that is
environmental information.

PART ONE — REQUEST FOR RECORDED INFORMATION

1. Whether the Council holds any recorded information created after the
2002 deposit — minutes, correspondence, reports, emails, photographs or
files of any kind — concerning Great House Farm (Ty Mawr) / Church View
Close, the village green in front of St Dochdwy's including registered
green VG 41, or the roadside verge by the churchyard wall.

2. Whether the Council holds any photographs, postcards or images of the
farm, the barn, the green or the church surroundings, of any date.

3. Whether the Council holds any recorded information showing what, if
anything, transferred to it from Penarth Town Council at the 1982
reorganisation, and any recorded information identifying where the pre-1982
Llandough community records were deposited.

If the answer to any of these is that no such information is held, I would
be content with a short statement to that effect — but I do need it stated.
Section 1(1)(a) of the Act requires the Council to confirm or deny whether
the information is held.

Section 10 (and regulation 5 of the EIR) allows twenty working days from
receipt, which on my request of 20 September 2026 I calculate as 16 October
2026.

If the Council is refusing, section 17 (and regulation 14) requires a
written refusal notice identifying the exemption or exception relied on;
section 17(7) requires the Council to give particulars of any complaints
procedure it operates, or to state that it has none, and to notify me of my
right to apply to the Information Commissioner; and regulation 11 gives a
right to an internal review of any refusal under the EIR.

"We have nothing more to add" does not meet those requirements. If the
period passes without a compliant response I will have no option but to
complain to the Information Commissioner.

PART TWO — MATTERS FOR THE COUNCIL'S DISCRETION

These are not part of the request above and carry no deadline. They are
simply things I would be grateful for.

A. I am not asking for the name or contact details of any individual. I am
asking whether the Council would be willing to pass my details to any
former member, former clerk or long-standing resident who might remember
the village between the 1950s and the 1990s, leaving it entirely to them
whether to contact me. I appreciate the Council may have data protection or
administrative reasons for declining, and I would not press it.

B. Whether the Council would be willing to table this correspondence at a
meeting and minute it. I am content for it to be tabled in full.

C. Whether the Council would consider, in due course, whether an
interpretation board or a plaque near the green would be appropriate. The
excavation on the land beneath Church View Close recorded 1,026 burials,
described in the published report as by far the largest early medieval
burial population so far recovered from Wales, above a Roman villa and an
Iron Age roundhouse. That history belongs to Llandough as much as to my
family, and there is nothing on the ground that records it. I would be glad
to give the Council or the community a short talk on the documentary
record, without charge, if that would be useful.

I should be grateful for a response to items 1 to 3 by 16 October 2026.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber/ Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

Provenance: this text is reproduced in the public GHF-E170 page as transcribed from the request quoted in the 28 September correspondence. The original sent-item email was not separately recovered in the reviewed public record.

PUBLIC TRANSCRIPTION — NOT THE ORIGINAL EMAIL FILE
Record: GHF-E106-R55
Date: 11 October 2026
Sender: Paul R. Egan, signed as Clerk to Llandough Community Council
Timestamp: not stated in the published transcription

Dear Mr Buckler,

Thank you for your email of  21 September 2026 making a request for 
information.

We are treating your correspondence as a request for information under 
the Freedom of Information Act 2000 (the act).

Under the provisions of the act and as defined by "The Freedom of 
Information and Data Protection (Appropriate Limit and Fees) Regulations 
2004" (the regulations) , an authority is not obliged to comply with a 
request for information if the authority estimates that the cost of 
complying with the request would exceed the "appropriate limit".  This 
appropriate limit is set by the regulations at £450 for our type of 
authority.

In the regulations our staff time is valued at £25 per hour.  This has 
the effect of imposing a time limit of 18 hours of staff time for 
activities specified in the regulations.

  The regulations make the following activities by an authority countable 
towards the cost limit.

  	* determining whether it holds the information,

  	* locating the information, or a document which may contain the 
information,

  	* retrieving the information, or a document which may contain the 
information, and

  	* extracting the information from a document containing it.

  We have estimated the time and therefore costs as provided by the 
regulations, and in doing so have taken into account the above 
activities.

  We estimate that this work will take in excess of 18 hours of effort by 
our staff. As we have a significant amount of documents on file from the 
period 2002-2016 where minutes are in documents rather than published on 
the website or in archives.

  We estimate this will exceed the limit provided for by the regulations 
and therefore your request is refused on the grounds provided for under 
section 12 of the act.

Our estimate of time is based on the requirement to search all minutes 
of the council and its committees for a period of 14 years. It is 
estimated that it will take about 20 minutes to read each set of minutes 
of which there are estimated to 224 sets of minutes. It is considered 
that this is likely to take about 10 minutes to assess each set of 
minutes a total of over 2240 minutes which equates to 37 hours.

  We may may be able to provide some information if you are able to 
reduce or refine your request to bring the cost of compliance under the 
regulations limit.  We suggest that you could limit the time frame of 
minutes that we would need to look through. For example 2002-2006.

  Please contact us if you would like to refine your request.

  If you are not satisfied with this response or you wish to complain 
about any aspect of the handling of your request, then you should 
contact us in the first instance and we will undertake an internal 
review.

  If after the internal review you wish to complain further then you can 
complain to the Information Commissioners Office http://www.ico.gov.uk 
[1] and request a decision notice.

The other matters you include in your email will be considered at the 
October meeting of the council and I will let you have the views of the 
council after the meeting.

Kind regards,

Paul R. Egan BA, Chartered MCIPD, CiLCA, F. Inst. LM, FIPSM
Clerk to Llandough Community Council
[Postal address, telephone details, standard privacy footer and quoted earlier message omitted.]

Dear Mr Egan,

Thank you for your email of 11 October 2026. It contains several separate matters, so I have answered each under its own number. Please respond to each separately. Nothing below withdraws or narrows my original request of 21 September, and attendance at a meeting is not a condition of my information rights.

I am not asking the Council to decide the family's title dispute or to make findings about any individual, and I am not alleging wrongdoing by you. I ask that records be identified, searched for and disclosed, and that the matters in section 4 be considered.

1. INTERNAL REVIEW OF THE 11 OCTOBER REFUSAL (FOIA s.12; EIR reg. 11)

Please treat this as a formal request for the internal review you offered, of the section 12 refusal of my request of 21 September. To the extent any information is environmental, please also treat it as representations under regulation 11 of the EIR 2004.

My request had three categories: (a) records created after the 2002 deposit concerning Great House Farm / Tý Mawr, Church View Close, the village green (including VG 41) or the roadside verge by the churchyard wall; (b) photographs, postcards or images of the farm, barn, green or church surroundings, of any date; (c) records showing what, if anything, transferred from Penarth Town Council at the 1982 reorganisation, and where pre-1982 records were deposited. I ask the reviewer to address:

(i) Scope. The estimate covers only the reading of 224 sets of minutes for 2002-2016. Please explain why that is necessary and sufficient for each category, particularly (b) and (c), and what other searches were considered: correspondence and email files, photograph collections, transfer or deposit records, any index or electronic copy of the minutes, and sampling.

(ii) Arithmetic. The letter gives 20 minutes to read plus 10 minutes to assess each set, which is 30 minutes x 224 = 6,720 minutes (112 hours), but states 2,240 minutes (37 hours), which is 10 minutes x 224. Please confirm which calculation was used and which activities under regulation 4 of the Fees Regulations it includes. I accept the limit is exceeded on either figure.

(iii) Section 12(2). Please say whether the cost of determining whether the information is held would itself exceed the limit, or whether the estimate concerns locating and extracting information once its existence is established.

(iv) EIR. The green, verge, trees, woodland and land boundaries are likely to be environmental information. Please say which parts were assessed under the EIR. The FOIA cost limit is not an EIR refusal ground; if regulation 12(4)(b) is relied on, please give the reasons, the public interest assessment and the presumption in favour of disclosure.

(v) Advice and assistance (s.16 FOIA; reg. 9 EIR). Limiting the minutes to 2002-2006 does not address (b) or (c). Please say whether any part can be answered within the limit and suggest a practical refinement.

(vi) Without prejudice to the review: if the refusal is maintained, please treat parts (b) and (c) alone as a refined request, assessed under the correct regime, so that no time is lost.

Please have the review carried out by someone who took no part in the original decision, with the outcome and reasons in writing. I would be grateful for the outcome within 20 working days.

2. NEW REQUEST FOR RECORDED INFORMATION (FOIA and, where environmental, EIR)

This is a separate request, not a refinement of the one under review. Please search for Council-held or controlled minutes, agendas, reports, correspondence, complaints, notes or referrals:

(i) from approximately 1986 to 1990 concerning Great House Farm / Tý Mawr, its occupation, title or tenure, development or demolition, including any concerns raised by my late father, William "Billy" Buckler, or other family members. I have family information that my father raised concerns at Council meetings around 1988, described within the family as fraud-related. I cannot verify whether he did, what was said or what followed, and I do not present it as established fact. I ask whether the Council's records can establish what, if anything, was reported, how it was handled, and whether it was referred to any other body;

(ii) of any date concerning the village green, roadside verge, trees and adjoining woodland, and any reported extension of Church View Close gardens beyond their boundaries into the woodland, including correspondence with the charity that holds the woodland, residents or other authorities;

(iii) concerning the 2002 deposit: please confirm whether the Council retains or controls any copies of the minutes deposited with Glamorgan Archives, and identify any record of that transfer, its date, and any archival reference or destination known to the Council. I am separately pursuing the deposited volumes with Glamorgan Archives.

I assert a proprietary interest in Parcel A and the adjoining woodland, but I do not ask the Council to adjudicate title. If nothing is held after appropriate searches, please say so. If anything is withheld, please identify the statutory basis and reasons.

3. SUBJECT ACCESS REQUEST (Article 15 UK GDPR; Data Protection Act 2018)

Please provide a copy of my personal data held by the Council, including data in minutes, correspondence, reports, photographs or other records (including retained historical records) concerning my presence at Great House Farm as a child, the events surrounding the family's removal and the 1988 demolition, and any later record that identifies or refers to me. An electronic copy, ordinarily without charge, is fine. If you reasonably need identity evidence, please tell me promptly what is required. I understand the one-month period under Article 12(3) runs from receipt of this request, or of any identity evidence reasonably requested. This section concerns only my personal data; my father's reported statements and the wider records are dealt with in section 2.

4. THE OCTOBER MEETING

Your email says my "other matters" will be considered at the October meeting. Please confirm:
- the purpose of that statement, and whether I am invited to attend;
- the date, time and venue, public attendance arrangements and any remote option;
- the agenda, item numbers and papers, as soon as available;
- whether my correspondence will be circulated to councillors, how decisions and any actions will be minuted, and how I can obtain the minutes or formal outcome;
- how I may make representations as a member of the public, including any procedure, deadline and speaking limit.
I have not yet decided whether to attend.

I ask that the following be placed on the agenda, as issues for clarification and not as findings:

(a) From my 21 September email: whether the Council will pass my contact details to any former member, former clerk or long-standing resident who may wish to contact me (entirely at their choice); table and minute my correspondence in full; and accept my offer of a short talk, without charge, on the documentary record.

(b) The green south of the former farmhouse: what the Council understands its present role to be (owner, manager, custodian or otherwise), and the recorded instrument, plan or Council decision on which that understanding rests. The family's research raises a question whether this land was distinct from the agricultural parcel addressed in the 1955 possession proceedings. I ask the Council to check its own records, not to decide that question.

(c) The woodland behind the houses: I understand the charity responsible for it has raised concerns that some adjoining gardens extend beyond their boundaries. I cannot verify that. Please establish the charity's precise account, whether the Council holds relevant plans or correspondence, and refer any substantiated concern to the appropriate landowner or authority. I do not ask for findings about individual residents without evidence.

(d) The 1989 planning record: the copy available to me refers to annexes containing representations from historic societies concerning Great House Farm, which appear to be absent. Please consider whether the Council holds copies and whether it will ask the planning authority or relevant archive to locate the complete papers. This matters to understanding what was put before the decision-makers following the demolition.

(e) The historic site today: a site visit and, in due course, the merits of an interpretation board or plaque addressing the farm, the archaeological discoveries (the excavation beneath Church View Close recorded 1,026 burials, above a Roman villa and an Iron Age roundhouse) and the history of the green.

The same distinction applies to my father's reported concerns and to my own claim: they are matters requiring clarification, not established findings. If any proposed action is outside the Community Council's powers, please identify the appropriate body.

5. CHARGES AND THE CLERK'S POSITION

I do not authorise paid searches or accept any charge, and ask that no cost chargeable to me be incurred without my prior written agreement. If the Council offers to comply for a fee (FOIA s.13) or proposes a charge for environmental information, please send an itemised quotation for consideration only (not acceptance): the legal basis, the work proposed, hours and hourly rate, the total, whether the work can be staged (for example, parts 1(b) and 1(c) first), any published EIR charging schedule, payment methods, payee, payment reference and deadline.

Your 11 October email is signed as Clerk, and I understood from public information that you retired from that post in June 2026. Please confirm: (a) whether you are currently Clerk, or acting or locum, and since when; (b) who is the Council's Proper Officer and who has custody of its records; (c) whether the 11 October decision was yours personally or the Council's; (d) whether any handover or inventory of records was made on a change of clerk; and (e) who will conduct the internal review. I ask only to establish who is accountable for the review and the records.

Please reply by email and by post to [… personal postal address withheld in public copy].

Thank you again for your time and courtesy.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Royal Signals Cyber / Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

[… personal postal address withheld in public copy]

1. PRESERVATION OF RECORDS

Because these requests concern historic records that may be time-sensitive for other proceedings and bodies, please:
(a) confirm in writing, within 5 working days, that all potentially relevant records have been preserved and that any scheduled disposal, destruction or retention-schedule review affecting them is suspended. I raise this as a precaution. For completeness, section 77 FOIA and regulation 19 of the EIR make it an offence to alter, conceal or destroy records with intent to prevent their disclosure once a request has been made.

2. INTERNAL REVIEW OF THE 11 OCTOBER REFUSAL (FOIA s.12; EIR reg. 11)

(iii) Section 12(2). Please say whether the cost of determining whether the information is held would itself exceed the limit, or whether the estimate concerns locating and extracting information once its existence is established. texts.wb-ce22924f:
Dear Mr Egan,

Thank you for your email of 11 October 2026. It contains several separate matters, so I have answered each under its own number. Please respond to each separately. Nothing below withdraws or narrows my original request of 21 September, and attendance at a meeting is not a condition of my information rights.

I am not asking the Council to decide the family's title dispute or to make findings about any individual, and I am not alleging wrongdoing by you. I ask that records be identified, searched for and disclosed, and that the matters in section 4 be considered.

1. INTERNAL REVIEW OF THE 11 OCTOBER REFUSAL (FOIA s.12; EIR reg. 11)

Please treat this as a formal request for the internal review you offered, of the section 12 refusal of my request of 21 September. To the extent any information is environmental, please also treat it as representations under regulation 11 of the EIR 2004.

My request had three categories: (a) records created after the 2002 deposit concerning Great House Farm / Tý Mawr, Church View Close, the village green (including VG 41) or the roadside verge by the churchyard wall; (b) photographs, postcards or images of the farm, barn, green or church surroundings, of any date; (c) records showing what, if anything, transferred from Penarth Town Council at the 1982 reorganisation, and where pre-1982 records were deposited. I ask the reviewer to address:

(i) Scope. The estimate covers only the reading of 224 sets of minutes for 2002-2016. Please explain why that is necessary and sufficient for each category, particularly (b) and (c), and what other searches were considered: correspondence and email files, photograph collections, transfer or deposit records, any index or electronic copy of the minutes, and sampling.

(ii) Arithmetic. The letter gives 20 minutes to read plus 10 minutes to assess each set, which is 30 minutes x 224 = 6,720 minutes (112 hours), but states 2,240 minutes (37 hours), which is 10 minutes x 224. Please confirm which calculation was used and which activities under regulation 4 of the Fees Regulations it includes. I accept the limit is exceeded on either figure.

(iii) Section 12(2). Please say whether the cost of determining whether the information is held would itself exceed the limit, or whether the estimate concerns locating and extracting information once its existence is established.

(iv) EIR. The green, verge, trees, woodland and land boundaries are likely to be environmental information. Please say which parts were assessed under the EIR. The FOIA cost limit is not an EIR refusal ground; if regulation 12(4)(b) is relied on, please give the reasons, the public interest assessment and the presumption in favour of disclosure.

(v) Advice and assistance (s.16 FOIA; reg. 9 EIR). Limiting the minutes to 2002-2006 does not address (b) or (c). Please say whether any part can be answered within the limit and suggest a practical refinement.

(vi) Without prejudice to the review: if the refusal is maintained, please treat parts (b) and (c) alone as a refined request, assessed under the correct regime, so that no time is lost.

Please have the review carried out by someone who took no part in the original decision, with the outcome and reasons in writing. I would be grateful for the outcome within 20 working days.

2. NEW REQUEST FOR RECORDED INFORMATION (FOIA and, where environmental, EIR)

This is a separate request, not a refinement of the one under review. Please search for Council-held or controlled minutes, agendas, reports, correspondence, complaints, notes or referrals:

(i) from approximately 1986 to 1990 concerning Great House Farm / Tý Mawr, its occupation, title or tenure, development or demolition, including any concerns raised by my late father, William "Billy" Buckler, or other family members. I have family information that my father raised concerns at Council meetings around 1988, described within the family as fraud-related. I cannot verify whether he did, what was said or what followed, and I do not present it as established fact. I ask whether the Council's records can establish what, if anything, was reported, how it was handled, and whether it was referred to any other body;

(ii) of any date concerning the village green, roadside verge, trees and adjoining woodland, and any reported extension of Church View Close gardens beyond their boundaries into the woodland, including correspondence with the charity that holds the woodland, residents or other authorities;

(iii) concerning the 2002 deposit: please confirm whether the Council retains or controls any copies of the minutes deposited with Glamorgan Archives, and identify any record of that transfer, its date, and any archival reference or destination known to the Council. I am separately pursuing the deposited volumes with Glamorgan Archives.

I assert a proprietary interest in Parcel A and the adjoining woodland, but I do not ask the Council to adjudicate title. If nothing is held after appropriate searches, please say so. If anything is withheld, please identify the statutory basis and reasons.

3. SUBJECT ACCESS REQUEST (Article 15 UK GDPR; Data Protection Act 2018)

Please provide a copy of my personal data held by the Council, including data in minutes, correspondence, reports, photographs or other records (including retained historical records) concerning my presence at Great House Farm as a child, the events surrounding the family's removal and the 1988 demolition, and any later record that identifies or refers to me. An electronic copy, ordinarily without charge, is fine. If you reasonably need identity evidence, please tell me promptly what is required. I understand the one-month period under Article 12(3) runs from receipt of this request, or of any identity evidence reasonably requested. This section concerns only my personal data; my father's reported statements and the wider records are dealt with in section 2.

4. THE OCTOBER MEETING

Your email says my "other matters" will be considered at the October meeting. Please confirm:
- the purpose of that statement, and whether I am invited to attend;
- the date, time and venue, public attendance arrangements and any remote option;
- the agenda, item numbers and papers, as soon as available;
- whether my correspondence will be circulated to councillors, how decisions and any actions will be minuted, and how I can obtain the minutes or formal outcome;
- how I may make representations as a member of the public, including any procedure, deadline and speaking limit.
I have not yet decided whether to attend.

I ask that the following be placed on the agenda, as issues for clarification and not as findings:

(a) From my 21 September email: whether the Council will pass my contact details to any former member, former clerk or long-standing resident who may wish to contact me (entirely at their choice); table and minute my correspondence in full; and accept my offer of a short talk, without charge, on the documentary record.

(b) The green south of the former farmhouse: what the Council understands its present role to be (owner, manager, custodian or otherwise), and the recorded instrument, plan or Council decision on which that understanding rests. The family's research raises a question whether this land was distinct from the agricultural parcel addressed in the 1955 possession proceedings. I ask the Council to check its own records, not to decide that question.

(c) The woodland behind the houses: I understand the charity responsible for it has raised concerns that some adjoining gardens extend beyond their boundaries. I cannot verify that. Please establish the charity's precise account, whether the Council holds relevant plans or correspondence, and refer any substantiated concern to the appropriate landowner or authority. I do not ask for findings about individual residents without evidence.

(d) The 1989 planning record: the copy available to me refers to annexes containing representations from historic societies concerning Great House Farm, which appear to be absent. Please consider whether the Council holds copies and whether it will ask the planning authority or relevant archive to locate the complete papers. This matters to understanding what was put before the decision-makers following the demolition.

(e) The historic site today: a site visit and, in due course, the merits of an interpretation board or plaque addressing the farm, the archaeological discoveries (the excavation beneath Church View Close recorded 1,026 burials, above a Roman villa and an Iron Age roundhouse) and the history of the green.

The same distinction applies to my father's reported concerns and to my own claim: they are matters requiring clarification, not established findings. If any proposed action is outside the Community Council's powers, please identify the appropriate body.

5. CHARGES AND THE CLERK'S POSITION

I do not authorise paid searches or accept any charge, and ask that no cost chargeable to me be incurred without my prior written agreement. If the Council offers to comply for a fee (FOIA s.13) or proposes a charge for environmental information, please send an itemised quotation for consideration only (not acceptance): the legal basis, the work proposed, hours and hourly rate, the total, whether the work can be staged (for example, parts 1(b) and 1(c) first), any published EIR charging schedule, payment methods, payee, payment reference and deadline.

Your 11 October email is signed as Clerk, and I understood from public information that you retired from that post in June 2026. Please confirm: (a) whether you are currently Clerk, or acting or locum, and since when; (b) who is the Council's Proper Officer and who has custody of its records; (c) whether the 11 October decision was yours personally or the Council's; (d) whether any handover or inventory of records was made on a change of clerk; and (e) who will conduct the internal review. I ask only to establish who is accountable for the review and the records.

Please reply by email and by post to [redacted].

Thank you again for your time and courtesy.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

The copy available to me refers to annexes containing representations from historic societies concerning Great House Farm, which appear to be absent. Please confirm whether the Council holds them and, if not, whether its records identify another custodian or archive;

(iii) of any date concerning the village green, roadside verge, trees and adjoining woodland: history, status, boundaries, maintenance, planting, public use, and any reported extension of Church View Close gardens beyond their boundaries into the woodland, including correspondence with the charity that holds the woodland, residents, the Vale of Glamorgan Council or other authorities. I am aware the official VG 41 registration file is understood to be held by the Vale of Glamorgan Council; I ask only for the Council's own copies, correspondence, representations and referrals;

(iv) concerning the 2002 deposit: please confirm whether the Council retains or controls any copies of the minutes deposited with Glamorgan Archives, and identify any record of that transfer, its date, and any archival reference or destination known to the Council. I am separately pursuing the deposited volumes with Glamorgan Archives.

I assert a proprietary interest in Parcel A and the adjoining woodland, but I do not ask the Council to adjudicate title. If any part is thought too broad, please identify that part and say what narrower search is practicable, rather than refusing the whole. If nothing is held after appropriate searches, please say so and identify any known transfer or deposit location. If anything is withheld, please identify the statutory basis and reasons. I understand the 20-working-day period under section 10 FOIA and regulation 5 EIR runs from receipt of this email.

4. SUBJECT ACCESS REQUEST (Article 15 UK GDPR; Data Protection Act 2018)

Please provide a copy of my personal data held by the Council, including data in minutes, correspondence, reports, photographs or other records (including retained historical records) concerning my presence at Great House Farm as a child, the events surrounding the family's removal and the 1988 demolition, and any later record that identifies or refers to me. An electronic copy, ordinarily without charge, is fine. Please acknowledge this as a subject access request. If you reasonably need identity evidence, please tell me promptly what is required. I understand the one-month period under Article 12(3) runs from receipt of this request, or of any identity evidence reasonably requested. This section concerns only my personal data; my father's reported statements and the wider records are dealt with in section 3.

5. THE OCTOBER MEETING

Your email says my "other matters" will be considered at the October meeting. You gave no date, time, venue or agenda. Please confirm within 5 working days:
- whether the meeting has already taken place and, if so, its date, the agenda and papers, the minute or other record of consideration, and any decision or action;
- if it has not, the date, time, venue, public attendance arrangements and any remote option, and the draft or published agenda showing which of my matters are scheduled and under which item numbers;
- whether I am invited to attend (I have not yet decided whether to) and how a member of the public may make representations on relevant business, including any procedure, deadline and speaking limit;
- that this entire email, and my earlier correspondence, will be circulated to all councillors, how decisions and actions will be minuted, and how I can obtain the minutes or formal outcome.

I ask that the following be placed on the agenda, as issues for clarification and not as findings:

(a) From my 21 September email: whether the Council will pass my contact details to any former member, former clerk or long-standing resident who may wish to contact me (entirely at their choice, and with no disclosure of their details to me without consent); table and minute my correspondence in full; and accept my offer of a short talk, without charge, on the documentary record.

(b) The green south of the former farmhouse: what the Council understands its present role to be (owner, manager, custodian or otherwise), and the recorded instrument, plan or Council decision on which that understanding rests. The family's research raises a question whether this land was distinct from the agricultural parcel addressed in the 1955 possession proceedings. I ask the Council to check its own records, not to decide that question.

(c) The woodland behind the houses: I understand the charity responsible for it has raised concerns that some adjoining gardens extend beyond their boundaries. I cannot verify that. Please establish the charity's precise account, whether the Council holds relevant plans or correspondence, and refer any substantiated concern to the appropriate landowner or authority. I do not ask for findings about individual residents without evidence.

(d) The 1989 planning record and the missing annexes (see 3(ii)): whether the Council holds copies and whether it will ask the planning authority or relevant archive to locate the complete papers. This matters to understanding what was put before the decision-makers following the demolition.

(e) My father's reported 1980s concerns (see 3(i)): that the Council consider what its own records show and, if they show nothing, say so.

(f) The historic site today: a site visit and, in due course, the merits of an interpretation board or plaque addressing the farm, the archaeological discoveries (the excavation beneath Church View Close recorded 1,026 burials, above a Roman villa and an Iron Age roundhouse) and the history of the green.

If any proposed action is outside the Community Council's powers, please identify the appropriate body.

6. CHARGES AND THE CLERK'S POSITION

I do not authorise paid searches or accept any charge, and ask that no cost chargeable to me be incurred without my prior written agreement. If the Council offers to comply for a fee (FOIA s.13) or proposes a charge for environmental information, please send an itemised quotation for consideration only (not acceptance): the legal basis, the work proposed, hours and hourly rate, the total, whether the work can be staged (for example, categories 2(b) and 2(c) first), any published EIR charging schedule, payment methods, payee, payment reference and deadline.

Your 11 October email is signed as Clerk, and I understood from public information that you retired from that post in June 2026. I treat that as unverified. Please confirm: (a) whether you are currently Clerk, or acting or locum, and since when; (b) who is the Council's Proper Officer and who has custody of its records; (c) whether the 11 October decision was yours personally or the Council's; (d) whether any handover or inventory of records was made on a change of clerk; and (e) who will conduct the internal review.

I would prefer to resolve all of this cooperatively and with the Council's full help. If the matters above are not dealt with properly, I will have to consider a complaint to the Information Commissioner (including on advice and assistance, the duty to confirm or deny and the EIR handling) and to the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales. I would rather not need to. Please acknowledge receipt of this email and each numbered part within 5 working days, and reply by email and by post to [redacted].

Thank you for your time and courtesy.

Regards,

Catalogue note — planning file for the houses built on the Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr land, Llandough-juxta-Penarth.

These are the Vale of Glamorgan papers for outline application 89/01396/OUT (also stamped 8901396 OUT). They are filed as PDFs under pdf/planning/ and listed in pdf/_treeview.json.

1. 1989-10-16 — Form D, Town and Country Planning Act 1971.
   Applicant: BP Properties Ltd, Britannic House, Moor Lane, London EC2Y 9BU.
   Agent: Debenham Tewson Ltd, 3 Castle Street, Cardiff CF1 2RJ.
   Land at Leckwith Road, Llandough, South Glamorgan, edged red, site area about 3.4 acres. Applicant's adjoining land edged blue.
   Proposal: residential development including a new access road. Outline permission. Siting, design, external appearance, means of access and landscaping all reserved.
   Buildings to be demolished: stated "None" (the farm buildings had already been demolished).
   Certificate A under section 27(1)(a), signed for B.P. Properties Limited, dated 16/10/89: certifies that at the beginning of the 21 days ending with the application nobody except the applicant was the owner of any part of the land. "Owner" means a freehold interest or a leasehold with at least 7 years unexpired.
   Application dated October 1989. Council stamp records receipt.

2. GGAT comments and recommendations on 89/01396/OUT (Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust Ltd).
   The church of St Dochdwy and churchyard are treated as an early Christian monastic site, possibly from about 650, with a tenth- or eleventh-century cross shaft.
   1979 Wales and West Housing Association development south of the church: emergency excavation found part of an Iron Age farmstead, a high-status Roman villa, a dark-age cemetery, a medieval monastic grange of Tewkesbury Abbey, a late medieval village, and a post-medieval mill and farm, none visible before development. Reference: Biglis, Caldicot and Llandough (ed. D. M. Robinson), BAR 188 (1988).
   Information on Great House Farm itself was limited to the record of the recently demolished property, listed as a county treasure. GGAT asked for a mechanical-excavator assessment under archaeological supervision, estimated at two weeks and £2,000.
   Policies cited: South Glamorgan Structure Plan (June 1989) EV15; East Vale Local Plan (February 1987) E9; Welsh Office Circular 61/81 section 26 (scheduled or unscheduled monument is a material consideration); SI 1988 No 1812 section 4; Circular 1/85 Appendix B (premature development should be refused).
   GGAT recommended that the authority not determine the application until BP Properties provided an archaeological assessment by a qualified archaeologist (IFA Directory 1988-9).
   Negotiations via Debenham Tewson had not produced agreement. Llandough Community Council had offered £100 if BP met the balance. GGAT noted BP were not the developer in the strict sense: they wanted to sell with outline permission.
   Appendix: extract of GGAT letter to J. Maitland Evans, 1 October 1982. Ty Mawr Farm (H2.1) was a three-acre residential allocation. "There remains a possibility that occupation continues to the north of the church; provision should be made, therefore, for thorough investigative work prior to the development."

3. Manuscript officer report (consultations include further GGAT comment dated 8 February 1990).
   Site described as about 3.4 / 3.5 acres adjacent to St Dochdwy's parish church. All buildings, including Great House Farm, demolished.
   Outline application; illustrative layout of 18 dwellings and access to Leckwith Road, matters reserved.
   Planning history: 8996/3337, 13 houses, same site, approved conditionally 25 July 1972.
   Llandough Community Council: no objection, but part of the land is a registered village green.
   Engineering: public foul sewer only; alternative surface-water disposal required.
   Cardiff Bay Development Corporation: no objection; retain trees on the north-west slope and the public right of way through the site.
   Welsh Water: applicant to liaise on foul drainage; a connection to the new Eastern District pumping main would not be permitted.
   Representations from the Barry Preservation Society and a county councillor (a member of GGAT), attached as appendices C and D (those letters are not in this scan).
   Applicant's agents replied to GGAT; that letter was appendix E (not in this scan).
   Most of the land allocated for housing in the East Vale Local Plan (policy H2.1). The policy said buildings on the site should be retained; they had been demolished a little while before. The remainder is inside the developed area. Sections are too steep. The site includes a registered village green (a very small area is also the subject of two searches) and is crossed by a public right of way.
   Recommendation: approve, subject to conditions, including the standard archaeology condition in Appendix B to Welsh Office Circular 1/85.
   Draft conditions include: structures only on level ground, not on steep or wooded areas; at least 0.1 ha (0.25 acre) beside Leckwith Road and the church boundary kept as village green / amenity; vehicular access at the north-western edge onto the A4055 with 4.5 m x 60 m sightlines; estate roads minimum 5.5 m with 1.8 m footways and 10.5 m kerb radii; public right of way along the north-western boundary not obstructed; retain the stone wall.

4. Decision, 13 March 1990. Vale of Glamorgan Borough Council. Application 89/01396/OUT.
   Outline permission GRANTED for residential development including a new access road at Land at Great House Farm, Leckwith Road, Llandough, Penarth.
   Application and plans received 8 November 1989.
   Reserved matters within 3 years; development begun within 5 years of this permission or 2 years of the last reserved-matter approval, whichever is later.
   Condition 5: 0.25 acres adjacent to Leckwith Road and the boundary with St Dochdwy's Church to be laid out as a village green / amenity area before beneficial use. Reason: to retain and enhance the existing registered village green.
   Condition 8: do not obstruct the public right of way along the north-western boundary.
   Condition 15: retain and make good the existing stone wall fronting the site, except where the access or building operations require otherwise.
   Conditions 16–18: archaeologist nominated by the authority may observe excavations; no development until a field evaluation and archaeological assessment by a qualified archaeologist, to be carried out within three months of the consent; detail plans must have regard to that assessment.

5. Plans bundle (one PDF, several dates).
   - Debenham Tewson 1:2500 location plan, identification only, stamped 8901396. Shows St Dochdwy's, the farm group, Llandough Moors and the surrounding streets.
   - Certified true copy of the register map, Deputy County Solicitor, 18 June 1985. Marks VG 41 and OBJ No 314 (LAND) at Llandough.
   - Heronhurst Homes exercise layout, Llandough, South Glamorgan, drawn 16.09.91, scale 1:500. Schedule: types E 3, F 3, H 3, W 4, Y 1, total 14. Net area about 2.40 acres. Shows St Dochdwy's Parish Church, village green, Leckwith Road A4055, and a public footpath.
   - Ideal Homes Wales / Wyn Thomas + Partners, job "Llandough Farm, Llandough", site layout 1, drawing 3024, March 1992, scale 1:500. Received by Planning and Development 16 December 1995. House types: Penlan 6, Sutton 9, Budworth 6, total 21. Village green to be maintained by Llandough Community Council and to form part of a pedestrian gateway to the Vale. Area to the north noted as to be maintained by the Forest of Cardiff Group. Penlan Road and a 5 m footpath are shown.
   - Fax cover sketch from Debenham Tewson, 29 January 1998, a further housing layout on Leckwith Road.

The outline consent is the planning permission under which the later housing layouts for this land were drawn. The 1972 consent (8996/3337) is the earlier permission on the same site recorded in the 1990 officer report.

Thank you very much for your enquiry. While we cannot advise you on a legal
case or undertake a review of historical decisions, pleas note that we do
hold information and archives related to Great House Farm, Llandough.



The site entry and description for the site in the National Monuments
Record of Wales can be seen online on Coflein, here:
https://coflein.gov.uk/en/site/20182.



We hold 14 archives related to the site, a list of which can be seen here:
https://coflein.gov.uk/en/site/20182/archives?size=25. These archives can
be viewed in our Search Room, located in the National Library of Wales,
which is open Tuesday through Thursday, 9:30-16:30. If you would like to
view the material in person, I would advise arranging with us beforehand so
that we can prepare the material ahead of your visit. Some of the material
is on microfiche and as we do not have a microfiche reader in the Search
Room, we will need to liaise with the National Library Reading Room staff
to try to negotiate the use of their machines ahead of your visit.



While it is possible to order scans of material using the attached order
form, we may be unable to provide research-quality scans or photographs of
some of the material, such as the material on microfiche, which would

able to provide scans or copies for personal, non-commercial research.

Sirs/Ma'am,

I am seeking representation and initial advice regarding the 1987 case BP
Properties Ltd v Buckler, which concerned Great House Farm, Llandough —
property long occupied by my family. I believe, among a myriad of
arguments, that the judgment was reached through a procedural inconsistency
amounting to bias or error in law, which may justify reopening under CPR
52.30 and Limitations Act Section 32.


---

Summary of the issue

In the 1987 case, the court ruled against my grandmother on the basis that
she did not formally reject an offer made by BP Properties Ltd, and treated
that as tacit acceptance. However, she had already explicitly rejected
prior licence attempts by BP Pension Trust Ltd, a related BP entity, before
BP Properties Ltd appeared as claimant.

The judge ruled that BP Properties Ltd was a distinct legal entity, and
therefore her prior rejection of BP Pension Trust Ltd’s offer was legally
irrelevant.

Later, in my father’s appeal, he argued that the wrong BP company had been
the claimant — that BP Pension Trust Ltd, not BP Properties Ltd, held the
relevant interest.
The appellate court dismissed his appeal, ruling that “BP companies are all
effectively one and the same” for the purposes of upholding the judgment.

This is a clear double standard:

When it benefited BP, the court treated the companies as separate.

When it benefited our family, they were treated as the same entity.


This contradictory reasoning — “heads BP wins, tails the Bucklers lose” —
represents either judicial bias, procedural irregularity, or corruption by
omission, and undermines the fairness of the original proceedings.


---

Grounds for reopening

Under CPR 52.30, a final judgment can be reopened if necessary to avoid
real injustice, in exceptional circumstances, where no alternative remedy
exists.
My argument is that:

The 1987 decision and subsequent appeal were tainted by inconsistent
application of corporate identity principles, creating real injustice.

The appeal court’s own language evidences bias and unequal treatment
between parties.

This meets the “exceptional circumstances” threshold.


Additionally, the Supreme Court ruling in Takhar v Gracefield Developments
Ltd [2019] UKSC 13 confirms that a judgment obtained through fraud or
concealment can be set aside even decades later — “fraud unravels all.”


---

Limitation Act 1980 – Section 32

Pursuant to s.32(1)(b):

> “Where any fact relevant to the plaintiff’s right of action has been
deliberately concealed by the defendant, the period of limitation shall not
begin to run until the plaintiff has discovered the concealment or could
with reasonable diligence have discovered it.”



I have only recently obtained and cross-referenced records revealing these
contradictions in corporate treatment and procedural handling — thus,
limitation does not bar action.


---

Requested scope of representation

Assess the viability of a CPR 52.30 petition to reopen or set aside BP v
Buckler (1987).

Review the documentary record (Land Registry files, local authority
archives, excavation permissions, HTV Wales coverage, etc.).

If viable, initiate a claim for rectification of title and potential
cultural property recovery of artefacts excavated during BP’s occupation of
the disputed land.



---

Attachments available upon request

Land Registry and microfiche title extracts (pre- and post-1987)

Local authority and archaeological licensing records (1985–1988)

Media and correspondence evidence of procedural bias and conflict

Chronology of BP company interactions with the Buckler family



---

Please confirm conflicts and whether one of your dispute resolution
partners can offer an initial consultation. I am prepared to provide a full
evidentiary bundle immediately upon engagement.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Kind regards,

Sion Buckler

Dear Mr Thomas,

I am seeking a preliminary opinion regarding potential grounds to reopen
the case BP Properties Ltd v Buckler (Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987),
concerning Great House Farm, Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan.

There appear to be two material issues:

1. Corporate Party Identification:
Correspondence relevant to the dispute was exchanged with BP Pension Trust
Ltd, while litigation and enforcement proceeded under BP Properties Ltd.
The Court treated these entities as separate when assessing notice but
effectively identical in dismissing the appeal and enforcing possession.
This inconsistency may constitute a mistake or misrepresentation under
Limitation Act 1980, Section 32.


2. Effect of the 1974 Letters:
The Court found that unilateral letters in 1974 granting a licence to
occupy rent-free for life converted possession from adverse to licensed.
However, I understand there is no evidence that this licence was ever
accepted. If acceptance did not occur, adverse possession may have
continued and the running of limitation may not have been interrupted as
the judgment assumes.


I would be grateful for:

Your view on whether these issues may be sufficient to apply to set aside
or reopen enforcement, or otherwise seek remedy or restitution; and

Your guidance on next procedural steps.


I can provide Judgment text and Newspaper records of the demolition (1988)
etc.

Thank you for your consideration.

Yours sincerely,

texts.wb-daaffdef:
Assuming I successfully reopen the case under the fraud and concealment exception in the Limitation Act 1980, s 32, win the case, and a court rules that the land, property, and artifacts were acquired by BP Properties Ltd through fraud, my claim and entitlement would be substantial.

Justice in this scenario would aim to place me and my family in the position we would be in, had the fraud not occurred (the principle of equivalence). 
This would likely involve a combination of the following legal remedies:

1. Recovery of Land and Property (Specific Restitution); The primary entitlement would be the return of the land and property to your family.
Vesting of Title: The court could order the current title holders to transfer the legal title of the land and any structures on it back to us, as the rightful owner. Possession: We would be granted legal possession of the site and the associated land.

2. Recovery of Artifacts ("Treasure" and other finds); The court would address the ownership of the artifacts based on the new ruling that the land was always rightfully ours.
Non-Treasure Items: Artifacts such as pottery, tools, etc., that do not meet the criteria of "treasure" would be legally declared our property as the landowner at the time of the find. Museums currently holding them would be ordered to return them to us (restitution).
Treasure Items: For items that qualify as "treasure" (e.g., the Roman coins), ownership legally vests in the Crown. As regards to our entitlement, while we would still not own the treasure outright, as the rightful landowner at the time of discovery, we would likely be entitled to:

Finder's Reward: We may be entitled to a full reward for the items' market value, which is typically split between the finder and the landowner.
Negotiation for Display/Ownership: A court ruling of fraud could strengthen our position to negotiate with the Crown or museums regarding long-term loans, permanent display with acknowledgment of our families ownership history, or even specific legislation for their return, similar to how historical restitution cases are handled for other cultural objects.

3. Financial Compensation (Damages and Restitution)
We would likely be entitled to significant financial remedies to compensate for losses incurred over decades.
Mesne Profits: This is compensation for the period the land has been unlawfully occupied. It would be the reasonable rental value of the property for the entire period of their possession.
Equitable Compensation: The court could award compensation for losses that were a direct consequence of the fraud and wrongful dispossession.
Account of Profits: In cases of fraud, courts can order the fraudulent party to give up any profits they made from the land that they were not entitled to (e.g., profits from its use or development), reversing their unjust enrichment.
Legal Costs and Expenses: We could recover the substantial legal fees and associated costs incurred by my father and ourselves in challenging this fraud, concealment etc.
Interest: Statutory interest would be payable on any awarded compensation from the date the loss occurred until payment.

4. Other Potential Legal Actions
Lien: A court could grant a charging order (a form of lien) against the properties or assets of BP to secure the payment of any substantial financial judgment awarded to us.
Moral Damages: While less common in the UK than in some other jurisdictions, the egregious nature of deliberate fraud and concealment might lead to consideration of damages for mental anguish, distress, and reputational harm, depending on how the case is argued and the evidence presented.

Summary of Justice
"Justice" in this scenario would be a formal acknowledgment by the highest court that a severe historical wrong occurred through corporate fraud, concealment, collusion, conflicts of interest etc - the list is extensive. The practical entitlement would be the physical return of the ancestral land and artifacts, combined with substantial financial restitution and compensation to restore our families standing. This would be achieved not by forceful acts, but through the due process of the UK legal system, following a successful review of the original case.

FORMAL NOTICE OF RECORD CHALLENGE, ASSERTION OF RIGHT, AND DEMAND FOR ENGAGEMENT

Dear Sir/Madam,

This Notice is issued for placement on official record and for reliance. It is not informal correspondence. I urge you not to resort to silence, deflection, or delay, as doing so following receipt of this notice constitutes knowing reliance upon, and maintenance of, records alleged to be materially defective through fraud, concealment, denial of due process, and systemic erasure. Please report any suspicious activity and discrepancies identified.

This Notice is issued in pursuit of narrative justice at this stage; formal judicial remedies are expressly reserved. It serves to document our family's side of the story before it is completely erased and history rewritten, ensuring awareness among custodians of land, heritage, heraldry, archaeology, and public records.

My elder brother, Rhys Buckler, and I are the sons of the late William Buckler (d. 1991), defendant in the landmark legal case BP Properties Ltd v Buckler (1987), and the grandchildren of the late Mary Williams, whose dispossession, marginalisation, and exclusion from judicial determination remain unresolved matters of record. Mary Williams was repeatedly and materially falsely addressed/mislabeled in legal and administrative records as "Mrs Buckler," a misidentification that was never judicially tested and which directly affected the handling, scope, and outcome of proceedings. The Williams/Buckler family held claim to the land title, having acquired and occupied Great House Farm continuously since 1667, based on family records, historical evidence, and centuries of resistance to adverse claims.

I place on record that I am the first member of my family able to speak publicly and formally on these matters. Other close family members remain too traumatised and intimidated by the historical conduct of these proceedings-including violent eviction, demolition, and loss of livelihood-to engage, despite the continuing consequences of dispossession. That silence must not be misread as consent, acquiescence, or abandonment of right. There is a material distinction between free silence and silence produced by fear, trauma, and coercive experience.

The story, as we have pieced it together, reveals a multi-generational pattern of lawfare and siege: from Norman/English conquests in 1100 granting lordships over ancient Welsh Christian landscapes, through monastic (1215-1539) and Crown seizures (1539 onward), to industrial encroachments (e.g., 1876 Limeworks severance without consent) and modern corporate possession actions. This culminated in the 1988 demolition of an 800-year-old farmhouse amid police standoffs, leaving the family homeless and the site scarred, now buried under Church View Close. Archaeological vindication came too late-1994 excavations revealed over 1,000 Roman and medieval burials, confirming family warnings (e.g., the 1870 Roman soldier discovery under the living room floor, suppressed by authorities)-yet heritage records celebrate the site while omitting our dispossession.

The following assertions of right are now formally placed on record. They have never been lawfully adjudicated or extinguished:

1.      Rhys Buckler may be the rightful Manorial Lord of the Manor of Llandough, by right of primogeniture and continuous hereditary connection arising from our family's occupation of Great House Farm from 1667 until our narrative, legal, and physical dispossession.
2.      I assert a claim to act as Squire of the Manor of Llandough, as executive representative and guardian of the Buckler-Williams estate and matriarchal lineage, with a mandate to pursue correction of record, restitution, and restorative remedies.

These are assertions of right, not settled declarations, placed on record pending proper adjudication-which has been historically obstructed through procedural narrowing, missing documents, and avoidance of full hearings.

In 1974, Mary Williams was twice prevented from presenting her case and obtaining a judicial determination of superior ownership, despite claims grounded in long occupation, intent, and possession. The court confined inquiry to animus possidendi (intention to possess) and excluded animus domini (intention to own), reclassifying her from putative owner to mere occupier and foreclosing title adjudication. BP sought possession only, not ownership rulings-a choice unexplained and significant. Proceedings were adjourned or quashed without resolution.

This occurred despite evidence of ownership intent, including:

*       Centuries-long occupation and resistance (e.g., failed 1938 auction due to local support; post-1945 rent disputes).
*       Roman-era remains and historical significance (e.g., Guglielmo Marconi's 1897 residence during radio experiments, with family aid erased from records).
*       Unformalized deals like the 1895-1905 Daniel Thomas quarrying permission for promised title, undermined by vanished deeds.

Judicial ownership examination would have engaged archaeological/heritage protections, incompatible with redevelopment-consequences avoided, raising credibility concerns.

Serious unresolved anomalies persist, indicating something is still not right with the record:

*       Licence correspondence dated 31 October 1974 surfacing only on 4 November, potentially interrupting proceedings to prevent hearings.
*       Claims of 1974 benevolent withdrawal under press scrutiny unsupported by verifiable coverage.
*       Land registration before Mary Williams's 1983 death without title determination; disputes possibly lodged/suppressed by Land Registry.
*       Inconsistent treatment of BP entities across proceedings to family detriment.
*       Procedural barriers preventing effective defense (e.g., interrupted essential services post-licence; 1960-1987 court rulings dismissing ancestral title as "notion" without evidence).
*       Knowing bypass of archaeological constraints (e.g., 1978 trenches ignored; no contemporaneous 1970s/1990s press on discoveries amid development).
*       Missing key documents (e.g., 1667 conveyance, 1811-1835 Lambert Williams agreements proving status, 1982-84 library deeds vanishing).
*       Risks of further erasure: Heritage databases celebrate "Llandough Roman villa cemetery" while omitting our saga; modern residents unaware of the "battleground" site.

These anomalies suggest systemic theft, from colonial English subjugation (e.g., 1543-1770 orbit shifts) to corporate siege, during Wales' cultural/economic transitions. Authority derived through such means is illegitimate under natural justice, customary Welsh principles, and moral-legal frameworks. The record's distortion secures advantage, but passage of time does not validate it.

Preliminary assessment indicates cumulative benefits from redevelopment (absent title extinguishment) exceed £100 million, forming a basis for reparations-covering lost land, artifacts, livelihood, and trauma.

I require relevant public servants, custodians, and office-holders (including Land Registry, heraldry bodies, museums, archaeologists, MPs, historians, and councillors) to cease delay, engage substantively, review/correct/annotate records where defective, and prevent further rewriting of history. Justice delayed is denied, especially with verifiable evidence available.

This Notice:

*       Challenges the record's accuracy, completeness, and legitimacy.
*       Place assertions of title/standing on record pending adjudication.
*       Reserves all rights without prejudice.
*       Puts officials/beneficiaries on notice that silence/reliance may aggravate responsibility.

For the avoidance of doubt, His Majesty the King was notified yesterday.

This serves as an invitation to engage constructively before reliance becomes untenable.

Regards, Sion Buckler On behalf of the Buckler-Williams family [redacted], Wales. https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/ <https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/>

Postscript - Disability and Succession (Material Notice): The heir-apparent to the asserted Manorial Lordship is Rhys Buckler's son, a young man with Down syndrome. Any obstruction, marginalisation, or differential treatment affecting his inheritance would engage the Equality Act 2010 and UK international obligations on disability rights. Disability cannot bar succession or recognition. This is recorded to prevent claims of ignorance.

Good afternoon,

Thank you for your enquiry. As noted in my email of 26 November last, while we cannot advise you on a legal case or undertake a review of historical decisions, we do hold information and archives related to Great House Farm, Llandough.

The site entry and description for the site in the National Monuments Record of Wales can be seen online on Coflein, here: https://coflein.gov.uk/en/site/20182.

We hold 14 archives related to the site, a list of which can be seen here: https://coflein.gov.uk/en/site/20182/archives?size=25. These archives can be viewed in our Search Room, located in the National Library of Wales, which is open Tuesday through Thursday, 9:30-16:30. If you would like to view the material in person, I would advise arranging with us beforehand so that we can prepare the material ahead of your visit. Some of the material is on microfiche and as we do not have a microfiche reader in the Search Room, we will need to liaise with the National Library Reading Room staff to try to negotiate the use of their machines ahead of your visit. However, I have located an electronic copy of Archive Number 6524751, which can be accessed here: https://www.walesher1974.org/her/app/php/herumd.php?group=GGAT&level=3&docid=301361628

While it is possible to order scans of material using the attached order form, we may be unable to provide research-quality scans or photographs of some of the material, such as the material on microfiche, which would require high-resolution scanning at a cost of £20 per scan. Moreover,  many of these records remain under third-party copyright, and we would only be able to provide scans or copies for personal, non-commercial research. Other uses, such as use in a legal case or report would likely require the permission of the copyright holder(s). I would therefore advise arranging to view the material in person rather than ordering scans, if possible.

Finally, I have confirmed with our Records Manager that we do not hold any correspondence related to the site.

Thank you again for your enquiry.

Sincerely,

Adam Coward

relied upon for that site.

In brief and as reflected in public records:

   -

   In *July 1974*, proceedings involving my grandmother and BP both
   asserting ownership, were adjourned and did not result in a judicial final
   determination.
   -

   On *31 October 1974*, a further listed hearing did not proceed
   substantively, following correspondence sent that morning by BP entities.
   No judgment on title was issued. My nan requested the audience with the
   judge the day before, with her lawyer. But that got leaked, the press
   descended on our farm (not that I can find evidence of news articles from

   our solicitor, effectively squashing the court hearing and audience with

   both BP letters (one from BP Pension Trust Ltd and one from BP Properties
   Ltd), that morning of the 31st of October, was also 'I own the land'.

   concerning land we asserted we owned, while the opposing party
continued to *assert
   ownership*, notwithstanding the absence of a concluded judicial finding.
   -

   -

   -

settled fact.

Yours faithfully,


Sion Buckler

Subject: Systemic governance concern regarding historic land registration and administrative reliance - BP vs Buckler 1987 (inc. BP Land Registry 1982)


Dear Committee Members,

I am writing to draw your attention to a historical land matter which I believe may illustrate potential vulnerabilities in public administration, record-keeping, and the governance of land registration. My purpose is solely to provide factual information for consideration, rather than to request remedial action.

The matter concerns land formerly known as Great House Farm, Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan, later developed for residential use and historically associated with BP v Buckler (Court of Appeal, 1987).

Chronology of relevant events (as reflected in public records):

  *   July 1974: Court proceedings involving my grandmother were adjourned without determination of ownership.
  *   31 October 1974: A subsequent hearing did not proceed substantively, following correspondence received from BP entities that same day. No judgment on ownership was issued.
  *   Throughout this period, my grandmother was not included in dealings concerning the land, while the opposing party continued to assert ownership.
  *   1982: The land was registered in the name of BP entities, despite unresolved competing claims and no final judicial adjudication.
  *   1983: My grandmother passed away after the registration, with ownership never conclusively adjudicated.
  *   1987 Court of Appeal: The record reflects an apparent inconsistency in the treatment of correspondence and corporate entities. Specifically:

     *   The court noted that my grandmother had replied to correspondence on 31 October, asserting ownership.
     *   The reply was treated as directed to the “wrong” corporation (BP Pensions Trust Ltd rather than BP Properties Ltd).
     *   In a later appeal by my father, the same judge acknowledged that both BP entities were effectively treated as the same for the purposes of the ruling.
     *   These circumstances resulted in the court upholding the opposing party’s registration despite prior correspondence demonstrating an assertion of ownership.

  *   Following these proceedings, my father’s application to the European Court of Human Rights was blocked.
  *   The family home was demolished, preventing re-entry, even for the retrieval of personal belongings.
  *   Despite its historical significance and a petition to protect it, the property was not preserved. The house had prior heritage interest, including documented connections to Marconi.
  *   1991: My father passed away at just 41.
  *   1994: The land was subsequently excavated, with items of archaeological interest removed.

Taken together, these events demonstrate a situation in which land registration and subsequent reliance by public bodies proceeded without definitive adjudication of ownership, raising questions regarding administrative safeguards, procedural coherence, and record integrity.

I am submitting this information purely for institutional awareness. I am not making allegations of misconduct, nor requesting investigation. I am able to provide a concise factual timeline and references to public records should it assist the Committee’s understanding.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler

*Kate Johal,*

I appreciate your prompt reply and thank you. I assure you I'm not out to
waste your departments or anyone's time. I just finished 22 years in Oath
in 2024 as a public servant, employed at the Vale of Glamorgan Council,
under the Welsh Government. I'm not only bona fine, I left my military
career beforehand - with honours. I truly believe I have the most
befitting case, that I understand your department specifically exists to
handle.

Is it not PACAC's role to ensure that the *machinery of the state*—the
courts, the Land Registry, and planning authorities—operates with
transparency and protects the constitutional rights of citizens against
administrative abuse? My case relates specifically to *maladministration*
and *constitutional overreach*: it involves the judicial "erasure" of a
320-year ancestral lineage through the tactical misnaming of Mary Williams
to "Mrs. Buckler", the administrative suppression of a known national
heritage site (the 1888 Roman find) to facilitate demolition permits, and
the suspicious disappearance of public title records from state-run
libraries. By focusing on how these public institutions failed to maintain
accurate records and fair procedures, I am  presenting a case of *systemic
failure in public administration*, which is the core reason I
understand your Committee to exist.

I must formally contest the assertion that this matter falls outside the
Committee’s remit. While the origin of this case involves a dispute with a
private entity (BP), the core of my grievance concerns *constitutional
issues* and the *quality of administration provided by government-funded
bodies*, specifically regarding the protection of national heritage and the
integrity of land registration.

I ask the Committee to review this matter under the following three pillars
of your mandate:

*1. Constitutional Issues: The Erasure of Customary and Indigenous Title* The
1987 Court of Appeal ruling (*BP Properties Ltd v Buckler*) created a
significant legal precedent regarding "unilateral licenses". My family
asserts that the administration of justice in this case allowed for the
tactical erasure of the "Williams" identity—a lineage with de facto
possession dating back to 1667—to facilitate a corporate land grab. The use
of the judicial system to overwrite centuries of documented continuity with
a "paper title" is a constitutional matter regarding the rights of citizens
against aggressive corporate-state interests.

*2. Standards of Administration: Suppression of Heritage by Public Bodies*
The Committee examines the quality of administration. My investigation
reveals that:

   -

   *Archaeological Suppression:* Evidence of a Roman soldier was discovered
   in 1888, providing "actual notice" of the site's significance. This was
   reportedly suppressed or ignored by planning authorities and the
   Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust (GGAT) to allow for demolition.

   -

   *Misrepresentation in Planning:* The 13th-century Great House Farm was
   administratively classified as a "dilapidated utility building" to bypass
   heritage protections.
   -

   *Missing Records:* Vital title evidence and Bute Estate deeds
   disappeared from the public library system—a failure of public record
   administration.


*3. Accountability of the Land Registry and Parliamentary Oversight* The
registration of this land under BP’s title occurred during a period of
transition in Welsh land law (c. 1982). If public registries accepted title
without disclosing active disputes or the presence of a known national
monument (the Roman/Medieval site), this represents a failure in the
"standards of administration" by the Civil Service. Furthermore, this
matter was raised in the House of Commons by MP Ted Rowlands in 1980, yet
the administrative failures continued unabated.

*Conclusion* I am not asking the Committee to act as a court of appeal, but
to investigate the *systemic administrative failures* that allowed a
historically significant site and a family's ancestral rights to be
"buried" through procedural maneuvers and the suppression of evidence.

If the Committee exists to ensure the Civil Service and constitutional
frameworks protect the public interest, then the demolition of an
800-year-old heritage site under a cloud of administrative "silence" must
be within your purview.


I look forward to your reconsidered response.


Sincerely,


Sion Buckler

suspect may be dispossession, fraudulent misrepresentation, and
archaeological suppression concerning my family’s ancestral land, Great
House Farm (historically Tŷ Mawr/Cedfin), Llandough.

possession and indigenous tenure of this land from 1667 until our forced
displacement in 1988. I am currently the only member of my family who is
not too traumatized to speak of these events. My mother (Mary Williams
daughter in law), remains to this day too terrified to speak up about this
multi-generational "lawfare" campaign waged against us. Our family have not
seen justice or received reperations, nor have we sued or reopened this
case under limitations act clauses of fraud and consealment. Yet. But this
may not be just a grave injustice upon our family, but our nations
archeological history and indigenous people on our ancestral birthland. We
are Welsh Nationals, Welsh speaking, under Welsh flags. This is some
British Colonisation-grade trespass I'm seeing and it's tandamount to a
declaration of civil war on me, my family, community and people.

concealment and fraud (see attached for my timeline and notes):*

   soldier in full armor beneath the living room floorboards. This discovery
   provided "actual notice" of the site's national significance a century
   before its demolition. We allege this notice was systematically suppressed
   by corporate and state actors to allow for commercial development.
   2.

   process, the 13th-century fortified manor was described by developers as a
   "dilapidated utility building" or "ruined barn" to secure a demolition
   permit that would have otherwise been denied under heritage protection laws.
   3.

   *Legal Identity Falsification:* In 1974, BP Pension Trust issued a
   "unilateral license" intended to bypass our possessory title. This
   correspondence was falsely addressed to "Mrs. Buckler" to bind my
   grandmother to her deceased husband’s name and legal status, despite her
   public rejection of their claim. She used her maiden name Williams and her
   husband Bucklers' intent to accept license died with him. My nan also
   alledgedly didn't expressly deny the offer and so accepted through her
   silence. But she was near enough voiceless from screaming for decades that

   if any. And to have responded to license to Mrs Buckler would have been
   identify fraud as she was Mrs Williams. And she did in fact reject BPs
   license offer and advanced, countless times, but publically. I believe
   these objections were suppressed too. There's allegedly news coverage from
   October 30th 1974 but I'm yet to find the evidence. But see attached a 1978
   article I unearthed. My nan clearly maintains her position "It's my home".

   4.

   that she might have responded to BP, but to BP Pension Trust, but the
   claimant was BP Properties Ltd which were two separate companies. But in my
   dads appeal when he challenges that BP Pension Trust Ltd should have been
   the claimant the same judge dismissed his appeal citing both BP companies
   are effectively the same. This is clearly a case of heads BP won, Tails we
   lost.
   5.

   our families deal with Daniel Thomas, for title after quarrying completed,
   in exchange for our permission to quarry, also disappeared from the loft of
   our home and the Cardiff Library according to my families accounts,
   precisely when they were needed to support our ownership claim in the Court
   of Appeal. Regardless we should have still remained on grounds we'd been
   there since 1667, and failing that on grounds of adverse possession.
   6.

   since 1888, BP profited from the land sale, the state and Crown have the
   exhevated artifacts and my displaced family are left traumatised, cheated
   and dead. My dad's appeal was dismissed to when it shouldn't have been and
   his ECHR request blocked, before dying abruptly at age just 41.

burials on the exact site of our demolished home proves that the "official
narrative" used to evict us was predicated on the concealment of known
facts.
